pageCache.text:
Modern Foreign Languages
Subject Statement
“At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, we believe that learning a language broadens horizons and helps children develop confidence, resilience and cultural understanding. Our French curriculum is designed to inspire pupils to become curious and enthusiastic language learners who are willing to take risks, embrace challenges and communicate with confidence. We celebrate the rich linguistic and cultural diversity within our school community and encourage pupils to develop an appreciation of France and the wider Francophone world. Through learning French, children gain valuable communication skills, cultural capital and the confidence to succeed in their future language-learning journey.”
Intent
At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, we aspire for every child to leave Key Stage 2 as a confident, curious and capable language learner with a genuine appreciation of different languages, cultures and communities.
As part of the Phoenix Federation, we recognise and celebrate the rich linguistic diversity of our school community. Many of our children speak English as an additional language and bring a wealth of cultural and linguistic experiences to school. We value these experiences and seek to foster a culture where all languages and cultures are recognised, respected and celebrated.
French has been carefully selected as our modern foreign language because it reflects both the international significance of the language and the diverse backgrounds represented within our community. Many of our pupils and families have connections to French-speaking countries, including Côte d’Ivoire (Ivory Coast), Cameroon and other parts of the Francophone world. Through learning French, pupils develop an appreciation of the cultures, traditions and communities connected to the language while gaining a broader understanding of the wider world.
Our ambitious curriculum develops secure foundations in listening, speaking, reading and writing. Through carefully sequenced learning, pupils develop their understanding of phonics, pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, enabling them to communicate with increasing confidence and accuracy.
We want pupils to become enthusiastic and resilient language learners who are willing to take risks, embrace challenges and understand that making mistakes is an important part of successful learning. Through language learning, pupils gain valuable cultural capital and develop the confidence and communication skills needed to thrive in an increasingly diverse and interconnected world.
Implementation
French is taught weekly throughout Key Stage 2 using the Language Angels Scheme of Learning. The curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure knowledge and skills build progressively from Year 3 to Year 6, enabling pupils to become increasingly confident, fluent and independent language learners.
Our curriculum is built around three key strands:
Phonics and Pronunciation
Pupils learn to recognise, reproduce and apply key French sounds and phonetic patterns. This enables them to read unfamiliar words with increasing accuracy and develop confidence when speaking.
Vocabulary Development
High-frequency and relevant vocabulary is introduced systematically and revisited regularly. Through retrieval practice, pupils learn to recall vocabulary from memory and apply it successfully in new contexts.
Grammar and Sentence Structure
Pupils develop an understanding of how French works. They learn grammatical concepts such as gender, articles, adjective agreement, verb forms and sentence structure, enabling them to move from single-word responses to increasingly complex phrases and sentences.
Across each unit, pupils develop skills in:
Lessons include songs, games, role-play, partner discussion, questioning, reading activities and independent writing opportunities. Teachers make meaningful cross-curricular links wherever possible.
Retrieval is central to our curriculum design. Previously taught vocabulary, phonics and grammar are regularly revisited to strengthen long-term memory and build secure foundations for future learning.
Assessment for learning is embedded throughout lessons. Teachers use questioning, observation, pupil discussion, written outcomes and end-of-unit assessments to identify misconceptions and inform future teaching.
Learning about France and the wider Francophone world is woven throughout the curriculum, helping pupils develop intercultural understanding and an appreciation of the rich diversity represented within our school community and beyond.
We maintain high expectations for all learners and provide appropriate scaffolding, modelling and opportunities for rehearsal so that every child can participate with confidence and experience success.
Listening and responding to spoken French.
Speaking with increasing confidence, fluency and accuracy.
Applying vocabulary and grammar in meaningful contexts.
Impact
By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils demonstrate growing confidence, enthusiasm and fluency as language learners. They have secure foundations in French and are able to apply their knowledge with increasing independence.
Most importantly, pupils leave Grinling Gibbons as aspirational, brave, determined, compassionate and enlightened learners who understand that successful language learning requires communication, resilience, practice and a willingness to take risks. They are well prepared for the next stage of their education and equipped to continue their language-learning journey successfully in Key Stage 3 and beyond.
Speak with increasingly accurate pronunciation and intonation.

Music
Intent
At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, we believe that music is a powerful and universal language that enriches children’s lives, nurtures creativity and supports personal development. Our ambition is for every child to develop a lifelong appreciation of music and to recognise its significance across different cultures, communities and traditions.
Through a rich and inclusive curriculum, pupils develop their skills as performers, composers and listeners whilst building a secure understanding of musical concepts and vocabulary. We aim to inspire children to express themselves creatively, explore their musical potential and develop the confidence to participate fully in musical experiences.
Music contributes significantly to the wider development of our pupils, fostering important life skills such as collaboration, communication, resilience, leadership and critical thinking. We believe all children should have access to high-quality musical opportunities regardless of their starting points and that every child should leave Grinling Gibbons Primary School with the confidence to see themselves as a musician.
Our curriculum celebrates diversity and promotes cultural understanding through exposure to a wide range of musical genres, traditions and influential musicians from around the world. Through this, children develop an appreciation of different cultures and gain the cultural capital needed to thrive in modern Britain and beyond.
Implementation
Our music curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure pupils build knowledge, skills and understanding progressively throughout their primary education. We use Kapow Primary Music to support the delivery of a broad and balanced curriculum, providing clear progression in musical learning from Early Years through to Year 2.
In Key Stage 1, children develop their understanding of pulse, rhythm, pitch, tempo and dynamics through singing, listening, composing, movement and performance activities. They learn to express their ideas creatively whilst developing confidence and enjoyment in music-making.
In Key Stage 2, instrumental learning forms a significant part of our music provision. Pupils in Year 3 learn to play the recorder, developing their understanding of notation, rhythm and melody. Pupils in Years 4, 5 and 6 learn to play the steel pans through specialist teaching, developing instrumental technique, ensemble performance skills, musical vocabulary and the discipline required to perform collaboratively.
Our renowned steel pan provision is a distinctive strength of music at Grinling Gibbons Primary School and has become an integral part of the school’s identity. As pupils progress through Years 4 to 6, they develop increasingly sophisticated instrumental and ensemble performance skills, enabling them to perform with confidence and musicality for a variety of audiences. The high standard of musicianship demonstrated by our pupils means that our steel pan groups are regularly sought after to perform at community celebrations, launch events and cultural festivals, including the Blackheath Kite Festival. These opportunities enable children to experience the excitement and responsibility of performing in public, helping to develop confidence, resilience, collaboration and a strong sense of achievement. Through these experiences, pupils gain valuable cultural capital, strengthen their connection with the local community and create lasting memories that enrich their primary school journey.
Singing is at the heart of our music curriculum. Pupils from Years 1 to 6 participate in regular whole-school singing sessions, developing vocal technique, musical memory, pitch accuracy and performance confidence whilst fostering a strong sense of belonging and community.
Our pupils also benefit from our valued partnership with Blackheath Halls and Lewisham Goes Gospel, participating in collaborative music projects, workshops and mass singing events alongside children from other schools. These experiences provide opportunities for pupils to perform in larger ensembles, develop their confidence, experience high-quality musical tuition and broaden their appreciation of the performing arts.
Performance opportunities are carefully planned throughout the year and form an integral part of our music curriculum. Children regularly perform to their peers, families and the wider community, celebrating their achievements and developing confidence as musicians. Our steel pan programme culminates in a vibrant end-of-year performance that showcases pupils’ musical progress and brings our school community together through celebration and shared experiences.
Through our listening curriculum, pupils explore music from a diverse range of cultures, traditions, genres and historical periods. In line with our commitment as a Race and Conscious Equality Charter Mark Beacon of Excellence School, we ensure that the music children study reflects the rich diversity of our school community and the wider world. This enables pupils to see themselves represented within the curriculum whilst developing respect, understanding and appreciation for the experiences and contributions of others.
Impact
By the time pupils leave Grinling Gibbons Primary School, they have developed a strong foundation of musical knowledge, skills and understanding. They can perform with increasing confidence, compose creatively and listen critically, using appropriate musical vocabulary to discuss and evaluate music.
Pupils demonstrate enthusiasm for music and take pride in their performances. They understand how music connects people, cultures and communities and appreciate its role in promoting wellbeing, self-expression and personal identity.
Through specialist instrumental tuition, collaborative music-making and high-profile performance opportunities, pupils develop confidence, resilience, discipline and a sense of responsibility. They learn how dedication and perseverance contribute to success and experience the pride that comes from achieving excellence as part of a team.
Our music curriculum equips children with the confidence to participate in musical opportunities both within and beyond school. Through high-quality teaching, specialist instrumental tuition and meaningful performance experiences, pupils leave Grinling Gibbons Primary School as confident, reflective and resilient young musicians who value music as an important part of their lives and the wider world.

Rights Respecting School
At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, we believe that every child has the right to be safe, heard, valued and inspired to succeed. We are proud to hold the UNICEF Rights Respecting Schools Silver Award, which reflects our commitment to embedding the principles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) throughout school life.
Being a Rights Respecting School means that children’s rights underpin our ethos, values and daily practice. Through our curriculum and wider experiences, pupils learn about their rights, develop empathy and respect for others, and gain the confidence to use their voices positively to influence change.
Our Rights Respecting approach helps to nurture responsible, compassionate and resilient learners who understand their role within an increasingly diverse and interconnected world. It also supports the development of positive wellbeing, strong relationships and a culture of mutual respect, enabling every child to flourish academically, socially and emotionally. To learn more about children’s rights, please visit the UNICEF Rights Respecting Schools website.
What are the Children’s Rights?
The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) contains 54 articles that outline the civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights that every child is entitled to, regardless of their background, culture or circumstances.
At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, these principles help to shape our approach to teaching, learning and personal development. As a Rights Respecting School, we are committed to creating an environment where every child feels valued, respected and empowered to succeed.
Our Rights Respecting approach has a positive impact across four key areas:
As a result, our pupils:
Our commitment to children’s rights is woven throughout our wider school provision. It is closely linked to our School Values, School Rules, Children’s Wellbeing Strategy, Zones of Regulation, and our work as a Race and Conscious Equality Charter Mark Beacon of Excellence School. Together, these initiatives help foster a highly inclusive culture where diversity is celebrated, every voice is valued, and all children are equipped with the knowledge, skills, and confidence to flourish both now and in the future.
This holistic approach ensures that children’s rights are not simply learned about but are lived and experienced every day through the ethos, relationships and opportunities that define life at Grinling Gibbons Primary School.
Feel safe, secure and supported.
Develop positive attitudes towards learning.
Build strong and respectful relationships with others.

What our Governors do:
Our governors are all volunteers drawn from the community, each bringing a range of skills, expertise and professional experience.
Our governors work alongside the school to support and challenge to make sure our children receive the best education possible. They are involved in the full breadth of school life and meet regularly with the school’s leadership teams.
Governors fulfil their responsibilities by:
Holding the school’s leaders to account for the educational and financial performance of the school. Governors create robust accountability for the school’s leadership team through rigorous analysis of performance data and financial information.
Setting the school’s vision and the strategy for achieving this vision. The school’s vision centres on pupil progress and achievement. Working with senior leaders, the governors agree key priorities and key performance indicators against which progress towards achieving the vision can be measured.
Ensure the school’s financial success and probity. The governing board must ensure that the budget that the school receives is managed effectively, and with regard to value for money.
Governors are appointed by the local authority except for parent governors, who are elected by parents and carers, and staff governors, who are elected by all school staff.

pageCache.text:
Art and Design
Intent
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that Art and Design is an essential part of a broad, balanced and ambitious curriculum. Through art, pupils develop creativity, imagination, self-expression and the confidence to communicate their ideas, thoughts and experiences in meaningful and diverse ways.
Guided by the National Curriculum and informed by the AccessArt Primary Art Curriculum, we aim to nurture every child as an artist, designer and creative thinker. We provide rich opportunities for pupils to explore, experiment, take risks and develop their own artistic voice through a wide range of artistic disciplines, including drawing, painting, sculpture, printmaking, collage, textiles, digital media and design.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced to ensure children progressively develop their knowledge, skills and understanding of artistic processes, materials and techniques. We want pupils to understand that art is not simply about producing a final piece but about exploring ideas, revisiting concepts, reflecting upon work and learning from the creative journey.
We are committed to exposing children to a diverse range of artists, designers, craftspeople, architects and artistic movements from different cultures, backgrounds and periods of history. Through this, pupils gain a deeper appreciation of the rich contribution that art makes to society and develop respect for different perspectives, identities and forms of expression.
As a Federation, we believe that creativity plays a vital role in developing curiosity, resilience and innovation. We encourage our pupils to be aspirational in their ideas, brave when taking creative risks, compassionate towards the viewpoints and experiences of others, determined in refining their work and enlightened through engagement with artistic and cultural experiences.
Implementation
Art and Design is taught through carefully structured units that provide pupils with opportunities to develop both substantive knowledge and practical artistic skills over time.
Using the AccessArt curriculum as a framework, pupils engage in a creative journey that allows them to explore materials, develop techniques, investigate the work of artists and create increasingly sophisticated outcomes. Learning is sequenced to build upon prior knowledge and experiences, ensuring children continually develop their understanding and mastery of artistic concepts.
A central feature of our curriculum is the use of sketchbooks, which act as personal creative journals. Sketchbooks provide pupils with a safe space to investigate, experiment, record observations, generate ideas, practise techniques, evaluate outcomes and reflect on their artistic development. They celebrate the process of learning and encourage pupils to take ownership of their creative thinking.
Throughout their learning, pupils are taught to:
Vocabulary development is explicitly taught, enabling pupils to articulate their ideas, explain artistic choices and engage in meaningful discussions about art and design. Through regular opportunities for critique and reflection, children learn how to analyse artwork respectfully and develop confidence in expressing their opinions.
Assessment begins with consideration of prior learning and is ongoing throughout each unit. Teachers use observation, discussion, questioning, sketchbook reviews and pupil reflections to inform future learning. This ensures that teaching remains responsive and that all pupils make progress in their artistic understanding and technical skills.
We are committed to ensuring all children can access and succeed within the Art curriculum. Teaching is adapted appropriately to support pupils with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and those learning English as an Additional Language, whilst maintaining high expectations for all learners.
Learning is enriched through engagement with galleries, museums, cultural organisations, visiting artists and creative experiences. Wherever possible, pupils explore the artistic heritage of their local area alongside significant national and international artists, helping them understand how creativity can shape communities and influence the wider world.
Cross-curricular links are carefully considered, allowing pupils to apply their creativity and artistic understanding across a range of subjects while maintaining the distinct disciplinary knowledge of Art and Design.
Generate and develop original ideas.
Observe closely and record creatively.
Review, refine and improve their work.
Impact
By the time pupils leave the Phoenix Federation, they will have developed the confidence, knowledge and skills to think and work creatively.
Through Art and Design, our pupils develop not only artistic skills but also the confidence to express themselves, the resilience to embrace challenge and the cultural awareness to appreciate the diverse creative contributions that shape our world. We aim for every child to leave the Phoenix Federation with a lifelong appreciation of the arts and the belief that creativity can inspire, influence and enrich their lives.

Computing
Intent: What We Want Our Children to Learn
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that a high-quality computing education equips pupils to use computational thinking and creativity to understand and change the world. Computing is an integral part of everyday life, and our curriculum aims to develop digitally literate, computationally minded, and responsible global citizens.
Our core ambition is for every child to see themselves as a digital creator, not just a passive consumer of technology. Our curriculum is ambitious, inclusive, and carefully sequenced from EYFS through Key Stage 1 and Key Stage 2, ensuring that skills and technical knowledge build progressively year-on-year.
Our Pedagogical Core:
Implementation: How We Teach Computing
Our computing curriculum is structured so that children know more, remember more, and can do more as they navigate an increasingly digital world.
High-Quality Classroom Instruction
Lessons are designed to be practical, rigorous, and explicitly modelled. Computing sessions maintain a careful balance of:
The Progression of Programming & Logic (Computer Science)
As pupils progress through the Federation, expectations shift dynamically from basic logical reasoning to text-based or complex block-based programming:

Online safety is not taught as a one-off annual lesson. It is woven into every single interaction with technology across the Federation. We teach children to navigate the digital world safely, critically assessing the content they consume, recognizing how to report concerns, and maintaining a healthy balance between screen time and real-world interactions.

English
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that strong literacy skills are fundamental to children’s success across the curriculum and beyond. Our English curriculum aims to develop confident speakers, fluent and enthusiastic readers and purposeful, independent writers.
High-quality, diverse and language-rich texts are central to our approach. Through reading, writing and spoken language, children develop their vocabulary, deepen their knowledge and understanding of the world and learn to communicate confidently and effectively. Our curriculum is carefully sequenced so that new knowledge and skills build on what children have previously learned. Key knowledge and skills are explicitly taught, revisited, practised and applied so that children develop fluency, confidence and increasing independence.
Reading
Reading is at the heart of the Phoenix Federation, and we want all children to develop a genuine love of reading. Children have access to a wide range of high-quality, diverse and language-rich books and reading materials that reflect our community and the wider world. Every classroom has an inviting reading area, and children have regular opportunities to read independently, read with others and listen to adults reading aloud.
Our teaching develops both word reading and language comprehension. Children are taught to read accurately and fluently while developing the vocabulary, knowledge and comprehension skills needed to understand increasingly challenging texts.
In EYFS and KS1, children are taught phonics daily through Read Write Inc. (RWI). Children learn to hear, say, read and write sounds and use these to blend words for reading and segment words for spelling. Children who require further support continue to receive targeted phonics teaching beyond KS1 so that gaps in foundational reading knowledge are addressed quickly.
In KS2, children take part in a daily 45-minute reading session using the Destination Reader approach. Carefully selected, high-quality texts are explored as a whole class. Teachers explicitly model reading strategies before children practise and apply these with increasing independence. Children develop their ability to predict, clarify, question, summarise, make connections, evaluate, retrieve information and make inferences, using evidence from the text to explain and justify their thinking.
Alongside comprehension, we explicitly develop reading fluency. Teachers model fluent and expressive reading and provide opportunities for children to reread and practise texts, developing accuracy, automaticity, appropriate pace and expression. Children who are not yet reading fluently receive additional targeted teaching and practice.
Reading for pleasure is promoted throughout the Federation. Adults regularly read aloud, introducing children to a wide range of authors, genres and texts that they may not independently choose. Children are encouraged to talk about books, make recommendations, explore different authors and develop their own preferences and identities as readers. Children are also encouraged to read regularly at home and share their reading with an adult where appropriate.
By the end of KS1, children should be able to:
By the end of KS2, children should be able to:
decode unfamiliar words using their phonic knowledge
read fluently, accurately and confidently
understand and discuss increasingly challenging texts
retrieve information and make appropriate inferences
use strategies to understand unfamiliar vocabulary
Writing
At the Phoenix Federation, we want children to become confident, fluent and purposeful writers who can communicate their ideas clearly and effectively.
We use the Luminary scheme of writing as a key resource to support the teaching of writing. High-quality, diverse and language-rich texts provide meaningful contexts for writing and expose children to ambitious vocabulary, different voices, styles and text structures. Writing opportunities have a clear purpose, audience and context, with children writing to entertain, inform, explain, persuade and instruct. Where appropriate, children also apply and develop their writing across the wider curriculum.
Our approach recognises that successful writing depends on children developing both transcription – spelling and handwriting – and composition – generating, organising and communicating ideas. These skills are explicitly taught and carefully sequenced so that children become increasingly fluent and independent writers.
The foundations for writing begin in EYFS. Children develop their spoken language and learn to compose ideas orally alongside the systematic teaching of phonics, spelling and handwriting. Children are encouraged to say and rehearse what they want to write before recording their ideas. As transcription skills become more secure, children are increasingly able to focus their attention on the content and composition of their writing.
Spoken language continues to play an important role throughout the writing process. Children discuss ideas, explore vocabulary and rehearse sentences orally before writing. Teachers explicitly model how writers generate and organise ideas, construct and combine sentences, draft, reread, revise, edit and evaluate their work. Shared and guided writing provide opportunities for children to practise these processes with support before scaffolds are gradually reduced and children take increasing responsibility for their own writing.
Children are taught that revising and editing are different processes. Revising focuses on improving meaning, vocabulary, sentence construction and organisation, while editing focuses on improving accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar.
We value quality over quantity. Children are supported to secure strong foundations in spelling, handwriting and sentence construction before being expected to produce increasingly sustained and complex pieces of writing.
Phonics and Spelling
In EYFS and Year 1, children receive daily systematic synthetic phonics teaching through Read Write Inc. Phonics supports both early reading and spelling by teaching children the relationship between sounds and letters.
As children progress, spelling is taught explicitly and systematically in line with the National Curriculum. Children develop their understanding of age-appropriate spelling patterns, rules and word structures and are given regular opportunities to practise and apply these within their writing. Dictation is used where appropriate to support children in applying their phonics, spelling, punctuation and sentence knowledge.
Teachers use assessment to identify gaps in spelling knowledge and provide additional teaching and practice where required. Our aim is for spelling to become increasingly accurate and automatic so that children can focus more fully on what they want to communicate.
Sentence Construction, Grammar and Punctuation
Effective sentence construction is fundamental to successful writing. Children are explicitly taught how to construct, combine and manipulate sentences to communicate their ideas clearly. Teachers model sentence construction and provide opportunities for children to orally rehearse, practise and improve sentences before applying their learning independently.
Grammar and punctuation are taught explicitly and purposefully. Children learn the grammatical knowledge and terminology outlined in the National Curriculum and, importantly, how this knowledge can help them control sentences and convey meaning.
Wherever possible, grammar and punctuation are explored through meaningful contexts, including the high-quality texts children read, sentence-level work, shared writing and children’s own writing. Our aim is for children to understand how and why writers make grammatical and punctuation choices rather than simply learning rules in isolation.
Handwriting
Handwriting is taught explicitly and progressively across the Phoenix Federation using the Letter-Join Programme. From Reception, children develop the physical skills, pencil control and accurate letter formation needed for writing. As they progress, children are taught appropriate letter joins and work towards handwriting that is fluent, legible and increasingly automatic.
Children practise handwriting regularly, and adults consistently model high-quality handwriting. Developing fluent handwriting is an important part of becoming an effective writer, as increasing automaticity enables children to focus more of their attention on the content and composition of their writing.
Spoken Language and Vocabulary
Spoken language underpins reading and writing. Children have regular opportunities to develop their confidence in speaking, listening and communicating their ideas clearly. They learn to listen and respond to others, explain their thinking, ask questions, develop ideas through discussion and adapt their spoken language for different audiences and purposes.
Partner and group discussion, oral rehearsal, storytelling, drama, debate, presentations and performances provide purposeful opportunities for children to develop their spoken language. Teachers model high-quality talk and support children to articulate increasingly complex ideas.
Developing a rich vocabulary is central to this work. Through high-quality texts, purposeful discussion and explicit teaching, children encounter and explore new vocabulary in meaningful contexts. Teachers explicitly teach the meaning and use of new words and provide repeated opportunities for children to hear, say, read and use them. Children are encouraged to be curious about language, make connections between words and select vocabulary carefully when speaking and writing.
Assessment and Inclusion
Our English curriculum is ambitious for all children, including those with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and children learning English as an additional language. Teachers maintain high expectations while making appropriate adaptations so that children can access and succeed within the curriculum.
Assessment is an integral part of teaching. Teachers use ongoing assessment during lessons, children’s independent work and appropriate statutory and school-based assessments to identify what children know, what they can apply independently and where further teaching or practice is required.
Children who are at risk of falling behind are identified as early as possible. Targeted teaching and additional practice focus precisely on the foundational knowledge and skills that have not yet been secured. This may include additional phonics teaching, reading fluency practice, vocabulary and language development, spelling and handwriting practice, oral rehearsal, sentence construction or targeted support with comprehension and composition.
For children learning English as an additional language, particular attention is given to developing vocabulary, high-quality talk, modelling and providing repeated opportunities to hear and use language. For children with SEND, teaching is appropriately adapted while maintaining ambitious curriculum goals.
Where children have gaps in foundational knowledge, these are addressed rather than moving children on to increasingly complex learning before they are ready. The impact of additional support is reviewed regularly and teaching is adapted accordingly.
English leaders work alongside teachers to ensure that the curriculum is implemented consistently and effectively across the Federation. Monitoring, professional development and ongoing support are used to strengthen subject knowledge, identify priorities and continually improve provision.
Our aim is for every child to leave the Phoenix Federation as an enthusiastic reader, effective writer and confident communicator, equipped with the literacy knowledge and skills they need for the next stage of their education and beyond.

Geography
Intent
At the Phoenix Federation, we believe that Geography helps pupils make sense of the world and their place within it. Our Geography curriculum inspires children to be curious about the diverse places, people, environments and processes that shape our world, whilst equipping them with the knowledge and skills needed to understand an increasingly interconnected global society.
We aim to develop knowledgeable, inquisitive and responsible geographers who can ask meaningful questions, investigate places and environments, interpret geographical information and think critically about the relationship between people and the planet. Through geographical enquiry, pupils learn to analyse, compare, evaluate and draw conclusions using evidence.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced so that pupils build their understanding progressively, beginning with their immediate surroundings, school and local community before extending their knowledge to London, the United Kingdom and the wider world. As part of this journey, pupils develop a strong sense of place through learning about Deptford and the local area, whilst also becoming informed global citizens who understand the similarities and differences between communities, cultures and environments around the world.
We are committed to ensuring that pupils encounter a rich range of places, perspectives and experiences. Our curriculum avoids simplistic or stereotypical views of the world and instead promotes understanding, respect and appreciation of diversity. Through Geography, children learn not only about the world they live in today but also their role in shaping a sustainable future.
Our Geography curriculum develops pupils’ geographical knowledge, substantive concepts, disciplinary thinking, vocabulary and fieldwork skills, enabling them to make meaningful connections across their learning and apply their understanding to real-world contexts.
Implementation
Geography is taught through carefully planned and progressively sequenced units that build pupils’ knowledge, understanding and geographical skills over time. Learning is structured to ensure that key concepts are revisited and built upon, enabling children to know more, remember more and make connections between prior and new learning.
Each unit clearly identifies the essential knowledge, vocabulary and disciplinary skills that pupils are expected to learn. Children are taught to think and work as geographers by asking questions, gathering information, interpreting data, using maps and analysing geographical evidence.
At the start of each unit, teachers assess and activate prior learning to identify what pupils already know and understand. This ensures learning builds on existing knowledge and addresses any misconceptions. Throughout lessons, teachers use responsive assessment strategies, including questioning, discussion and retrieval practice, to monitor understanding. Learning is further assessed through the use of exit tickets, which provide valuable insights into pupils’ knowledge acquisition and inform subsequent teaching.
Fieldwork is a central aspect of our Geography curriculum. Wherever possible, pupils engage in practical and first-hand experiences that allow them to observe, investigate and interpret the world around them. Our unique location provides valuable opportunities for children to study Deptford, Lewisham, London and the River Thames, strengthening their understanding of local geography whilst making meaningful comparisons with national and global locations.
Vocabulary development is prioritised throughout the curriculum. Through discussion, oracy activities and enquiry-based learning, pupils develop confidence in using increasingly sophisticated geographical language to explain their thinking and communicate their understanding effectively.
Teachers adapt learning to ensure all pupils, including those with SEND, disadvantaged pupils and those with EAL, can access an ambitious curriculum and achieve success. Appropriate scaffolds, support and challenge are provided so that every child can participate fully in geographical learning.
Cross-curricular links are made thoughtfully with subjects such as English, Mathematics, Science, Computing and Art where they enhance learning. However, the distinct disciplinary knowledge and skills of Geography remain central to the curriculum.
Throughout their learning, pupils explore important themes such as sustainability, environmental responsibility, climate change, global interdependence and human impact, developing an understanding of both local and global issues.
Impact
By the time pupils leave the Phoenix Federation, they will have developed a secure body of geographical knowledge and a deep understanding of the relationships between people, places and environments.
Through Geography, our pupils leave us as informed, curious and compassionate global citizens who understand both their local community and their place within the wider world. They possess the knowledge, skills and awareness needed to engage positively with the opportunities and challenges of the future and are well prepared for the next stage of their education.

History
Intent
At The Phoenix Federation, we aim to inspire pupils with a curiosity and fascination about the past that will remain with them throughout their lives. Our history curriculum is designed to help children develop a secure understanding of Britain’s past and that of the wider world, enabling them to make sense of the present and understand how societies have evolved over time.
We provide a broad, ambitious and knowledge-rich curriculum that develops pupils’ understanding of chronology, significant events, influential individuals and diverse civilisations. Through carefully planned learning experiences, pupils gain both substantive knowledge (what happened in the past) and disciplinary knowledge (how historians investigate, analyse and interpret the past).
Our curriculum reflects the diversity of Britain and the wider world by exploring the lives, achievements and experiences of people from a wide range of cultures, backgrounds and communities throughout history. Through the study of local, national and global history, pupils develop an appreciation of how different societies have shaped the world we live in today.
We believe that local history plays a vital role in helping pupils understand their own identity, community and place within society. Through the study of significant local events, including the New Cross Fire of 1981, pupils develop an understanding of the experiences, contributions and challenges that have shaped the communities they live in today. This helps pupils make meaningful connections between the past and present whilst fostering empathy, reflection and a sense of belonging.
We promote inclusivity and high expectations for all learners. Drawing on evidence-informed approaches championed by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), we ensure that all pupils, including disadvantaged pupils and those with SEND, are supported to access ambitious historical learning and achieve success.
Implementation
History is taught through a carefully sequenced curriculum that builds knowledge and skills progressively from Early Years through to Year 6. Learning is organised so that pupils revisit and deepen their understanding of key historical concepts, enabling them to make meaningful connections across different periods, civilisations and geographical locations.
Teaching focuses on acquiring and retaining important historical knowledge while developing pupils’ ability to think and work as historians. Children are taught to:
Our teaching reflects EEF-informed approaches to effective learning. Key vocabulary is explicitly taught and revisited throughout each unit and over time. Prior learning is regularly revisited through retrieval practice, helping pupils transfer knowledge from their working memory into their long-term memory and enabling them to make meaningful connections between new and existing learning.
Assessment for learning is embedded throughout the curriculum. Teachers use skilled questioning, discussion, observation, written work, low-stakes quizzes and exit tickets to check pupils’ understanding, identify misconceptions and inform future teaching. Exit tickets provide valuable opportunities for pupils to reflect on and demonstrate what they have learned, enabling teachers to respond precisely to pupils’ needs and ensure that knowledge is secured over time.
History learning culminates in purposeful outcomes that allow pupils to synthesise and communicate their understanding. Pupils regularly complete extended pieces of writing, including historical narratives, non-chronological reports, biographies, balanced arguments and newspaper reports. These outcomes provide opportunities for children to apply historical knowledge, use precise disciplinary vocabulary and demonstrate their understanding of chronology, cause and consequence, significance and interpretation. Such work allows pupils to showcase their historical learning whilst further developing their communication and literacy skills.
History is enriched through educational visits, local history studies, artefacts, visitors, high-quality texts and cross-curricular links that bring learning to life. A significant aspect of our local history offer is the study of the New Cross Fire of 1981, an important event in the history of Lewisham and the wider Black British community. Pupils have opportunities to visit the New Cross Fire Memorial, engage with local historical sources and hear first-hand accounts from family and community members whose experiences help bring this history to life.
These experiences deepen pupils’ understanding of remembrance, community activism, equality and social justice whilst developing their ability to work with different forms of historical evidence. They also provide valuable cultural capital, helping pupils make meaningful connections between historical learning, their local community and the wider world.
Learning is carefully scaffolded where necessary whilst maintaining high levels of challenge and ambition for all pupils.

Impact
The impact of our history curriculum is that pupils leave The Phoenix Federation with a secure body of historical knowledge and a genuine enthusiasm for learning about the past. They can discuss historical events, people and periods with increasing confidence, accuracy and sophistication.
They understand how historians construct knowledge about the past and can use evidence to form, justify and evaluate their own conclusions.
Assessment is used effectively to ensure knowledge is remembered, connected and built upon over time. Through a range of formative and summative assessment strategies, teachers monitor pupils’ understanding and identify next steps in learning.
As a result, pupils are able to recall and apply previously taught historical knowledge with increasing confidence and accuracy. They know more, remember more and develop a deeper understanding of key historical concepts, historical enquiry and the connections between different periods of time.
Pupils develop a strong understanding of their local area and its history. They recognise how local events connect to national and global themes and understand that the experiences and voices of individuals and communities play an important role in shaping historical narratives.
Our pupils leave the Federation as knowledgeable, reflective and inquisitive learners who are well prepared for the next stage of their education. They possess the historical knowledge, enquiry skills and cultural understanding needed to become informed, thoughtful and active citizens.
Our history curriculum is underpinned by evidence-informed practice, including EEF recommendations on high-quality teaching, vocabulary development, retrieval practice, metacognition, and effective implementation. It reflects Ofsted’s focus on a well-designed curriculum in which pupils acquire, remember and connect important knowledge over time, enabling them to know more, remember more and understand more.
Secure chronological understanding.

Subject Statement
“At The Phoenix Federation, we believe that history helps children understand who they are, where they come from and how the world around them has been shaped. Through an ambitious, knowledge-rich curriculum, pupils develop the skills to think critically, analyse evidence, and appreciate different perspectives. We want our children to become curious historians who ask thoughtful questions, challenge assumptions and develop a lifelong fascination with the past. By exploring local, national and global history, including significant events such as the New Cross Fire of 1981, pupils gain the knowledge, confidence and cultural understanding needed to become informed, reflective and active citizens of the future.”

Maths
Intent
At The Phoenix Federation, we believe that every child can learn, enjoy and succeed in mathematics. We are committed to providing a mathematics curriculum that is ambitious, inclusive and accessible to all. Every pupil, regardless of their starting point, background or individual need, is encouraged and supported to develop confidence, competence and a positive mathematical identity.
We want our children to see themselves as mathematicians: curious, resilient and willing to explore ideas, make connections, explain their thinking and learn from mistakes. We believe that mistakes are an essential part of learning and that productive struggle helps children develop deeper mathematical understanding and greater resilience.
Mathematics is a creative and highly interconnected discipline. It is essential to everyday life, central to science, technology and engineering, important for financial literacy and vital to many forms of future study and employment. For this reason, our mathematics curriculum extends beyond learning calculation methods. We want pupils to understand why mathematics works, recognise relationships and patterns, select efficient strategies, reason logically and apply their knowledge confidently to unfamiliar situations.
We recognise that mathematics is a universal language that transcends cultures, countries and time periods, and we want children to understand that many different cultures and civilisations have shaped mathematical thinking and innovation throughout history.
We celebrate the rich linguistic and cultural diversity of our community and believe that all children can achieve highly in mathematics. Mathematical discussion, reasoning and explanation provide opportunities for pupils to communicate their thinking, learn from one another and develop confidence in their mathematical voice.
Through a high-quality mathematics education, our pupils develop the knowledge, skills, language and confidence they need to succeed in school and in the wider world.
Our mathematics curriculum is designed to ensure that all pupils develop:
Our curriculum fulfils the requirements of the National Curriculum. It is informed by evidence-informed practice, including guidance from the National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics (NCETM) and the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF).
The National Curriculum identifies three interconnected aims: pupils should become fluent in the fundamentals of mathematics, reason mathematically and solve increasingly complex problems. These principles underpin our curriculum from the Early Years through to Year 6.
Through our high expectations and inclusive approach, we aim for every child to leave primary school as a confident and capable mathematician, fully prepared for the next stage of their education.
Fluency in key number facts and calculation.
Precise mathematical vocabulary.
Confidence in explaining and justifying their thinking.
The ability to reason mathematically.
Effective strategies for solving problems.
Resilience when mathematics becomes challenging.
Implementation
At The Phoenix Federation, we have high expectations for all pupils. We do not view mathematical ability as fixed. Children are supported to understand that success in mathematics requires thinking, practice, perseverance, and a willingness to learn from mistakes.
Mathematics is taught daily through an evidence-informed approach based upon the principles of Teaching for Mastery, guidance from the NCETM and recommendations from the EEF.
Learning is carefully sequenced so that new knowledge builds upon what pupils already know. Complex concepts are broken into smaller, connected steps, allowing pupils to develop secure understanding before moving forward.
Teachers continually consider:
Teaching is responsive. Teachers use questioning, observation, discussion, retrieval activities and pupils’ work to identify understanding and misconceptions and adapt teaching accordingly.
What do pupils already know?
What do they need to learn next?
What mathematical structure needs to be understood?
Which representation will make that structure visible?
What misconceptions might occur?
Teaching and Learning
Teaching follows a Gradual Release of Responsibility (GRR) approach, moving pupils from teacher modelling, through guided practice and collaborative discussion, towards increasing independence. This enables pupils to develop confidence, deepen understanding and apply new learning successfully.
Through carefully structured lessons, children are supported to rehearse, explain and refine their thinking before demonstrating their understanding independently. This ensures that all pupils are appropriately supported whilst maintaining high expectations and challenge.
Teaching for Mastery
Teaching for Mastery is at the heart of our mathematics curriculum. Through our involvement with NCETM Maths Hubs and ongoing professional development, teachers continually develop their subject knowledge and pedagogical expertise.
Our approach is informed by the Five Big Ideas of Teaching for Mastery:
Coherence
Learning is broken into small, connected steps that build understanding over time.
Representation and Structure
Manipulatives, images and models are carefully selected to help pupils see and understand mathematical structures.
Mathematical Thinking
Pupils notice patterns, make connections, reason, explain, generalise and justify their thinking.
Fluency
Pupils develop secure recall alongside conceptual understanding and flexible, efficient strategies.
Variation
Examples and questions are carefully chosen to help pupils notice what changes, what remains the same and why.
Teaching for Mastery enables all children to develop a deep, secure and adaptable understanding of mathematics. Rather than accelerating pupils through content, we focus on securing understanding, making connections and developing mathematical reasoning.
White Rose Maths
Our curriculum is coherently sequenced from the Early Years to Year 6 so that knowledge and skills build systematically over time.
White Rose Maths provides an important planning spine. Teachers use White Rose Schemes of Learning alongside high-quality resources from NCETM, NRICH, carefully selected real-life mathematical contexts and responsive assessment information. These resources are adapted to meet our pupils’ needs while maintaining ambition and coherence.
Key concepts are deliberately revisited and developed with increasing depth, helping pupils retain knowledge, make connections and apply previous learning to new mathematical situations.

Numberblocks
Strong foundations in mathematics begin in the Early Years. In EYFS and Key Stage 1, we utilise Numberblocks as part of our mathematical provision. Mathematics is integrated throughout the day through purposeful adult-led teaching, practical experiences, discussion and play. Children develop mathematical language, reasoning and number sense through rich and engaging experiences. Numberblocks supports pupils in visualising mathematical concepts and developing a deep understanding of number structures, patterns and relationships.
Fluency
Secure number knowledge provides the foundation for later mathematical success. At The Phoenix Federation, fluency is developed alongside reasoning and problem solving through carefully sequenced learning, retrieval practice, mathematical discussion and purposeful practice. Pupils develop automatic recall of key facts whilst also understanding the mathematical structures and relationships that underpin them. Regular retrieval opportunities ensure previously taught concepts, methods and number facts are revisited and strengthened, helping pupils develop secure long-term mathematical understanding.
To achieve this, we have a whole-school approach to the teaching and learning of multiplication facts. This focuses on carefully sequenced key facts that enable children to develop a deep and embedded understanding of multiplication and division relationships. These sessions take place regularly throughout the week, particularly in Lower Key Stage 2, ensuring pupils are fully prepared for future mathematical learning, including the Multiplication Tables Check. To further support fluency, retrieval and independent practice, pupils regularly use Times Tables Rock Stars (TTRS) and Mathletics. These platforms provide engaging opportunities for pupils to practise multiplication and division facts, consolidate previously taught learning and apply mathematical skills independently. Through regular use, pupils strengthen their recall of key facts, increase confidence and accuracy when working with number, and develop greater fluency across the mathematics curriculum. This enables pupils to focus more fully on reasoning, problem solving and deeper mathematical thinking.
Mathematical Vocabulary and Oracy
Language is fundamental to mathematical understanding. Mathematical vocabulary is explicitly introduced, modelled, displayed, revisited and used throughout lessons. Teachers model complete mathematical explanations and give pupils opportunities to rehearse mathematical language through discussion with adults and peers.
Pupils are encouraged to use increasingly precise vocabulary when describing relationships, explaining methods and justifying conclusions. Sentence stems and structured mathematical talk support children in organising and communicating their thinking.
This supports pupils in articulating increasingly complex mathematical ideas and enables teachers to assess the depth of pupils’ understanding.
To further strengthen mathematical communication, pupils regularly explore key vocabulary using Frayer Models. This approach encourages children to define mathematical concepts, identify examples and non-examples, make connections and deepen their conceptual understanding. By explicitly teaching vocabulary in this way, pupils are better equipped to discuss mathematical ideas accurately and confidently.

Reflection and Mathematical Thinking
At The Phoenix Federation, pupils are encouraged to reflect on their learning and develop an awareness of how they learn most effectively.
At the end of lessons, children regularly complete mathematical summaries and reflections which encourage them to consolidate key learning, identify important mathematical ideas and make connections to previous learning.
These reflections provide valuable opportunities for pupils to articulate their thinking, explain chosen strategies and evaluate their understanding. This supports the development of metacognitive skills and enables pupils to become increasingly reflective, independent and confident mathematicians.
Inclusion and Challenge
Our mathematics curriculum is inclusive and ambitious for all learners, including pupils with SEND.
Teachers identify barriers to mathematical learning and make adaptations that enable pupils to participate successfully whilst maintaining appropriately high expectations.
Adaptations may include:
Where pupils have highly individualised learning needs, mathematical provision is appropriately adapted whilst remaining ambitious and focused upon meaningful progress from individual starting points.
Pupils who grasp concepts rapidly are challenged through deeper reasoning, problem solving and opportunities to make wider mathematical connections.
Structured mathematical discussion, reflection activities and carefully chosen representations ensure that all pupils can access ambitious mathematical learning and communicate their thinking successfully.

Impact
The impact of our mathematics curriculum is evident in the confidence, resilience and mathematical understanding demonstrated by our pupils.
By the time pupils leave The Phoenix Federation, they:
Assessment information, retrieval opportunities, lesson observations, pupil discussion, mathematical reflections and summaries demonstrate that pupils build secure mathematical knowledge over time and are increasingly able to recall, connect and apply learning independently.
As a result, pupils know more, remember more and develop a deep, secure and adaptable understanding of mathematics.
Our pupils leave The Phoenix Federation as confident mathematicians who appreciate the relevance, beauty and power of mathematics. They are fully prepared for the next stage of their education and equipped with the mathematical knowledge, skills and self-belief needed to thrive in school and beyond.

Phonics – Read Write Inc.
At Grinling Gibbons Primary School, we are committed to ensuring that every child becomes a confident, fluent and enthusiastic reader. We use Read Write Inc. (RWI) as our systematic synthetic phonics programme, providing a consistent approach to phonics, early reading and spelling.
Intent
Our intention is for every child to become a successful, confident and independent reader, regardless of their starting point or individual needs.
Our phonics curriculum aims to:
Develop secure phoneme-grapheme knowledge.
Develop reading fluency, accuracy and confidence.
Implementation
Nursery
Children’s phonics journey begins in Nursery, where they develop the foundations for reading through listening, speaking, rhyme, rhythm, vocabulary and sound discrimination.
Reception
Children begin systematic Read Write Inc. phonics, learning sounds and graphemes and applying these through blending, decoding, spelling and reading. Children are grouped according to their current phonic knowledge, ensuring teaching is appropriately targeted.
Years 1 and 2
Phonics continues systematically, with children consolidating their knowledge and applying it to reading and spelling. Regular assessment ensures that gaps are identified and addressed promptly.
Children read decodable books matched to the sounds they have been taught, allowing them to practise their skills successfully and develop independence.
Home Reading
In EYFS and KS1, children take home a decodable book matched to their phonics knowledge, alongside a book to enjoy and share with parents or carers, supporting both reading practice and a love of reading.
Phonics Screening Check
In Year 1, children complete the statutory Phonics Screening Check. We use this alongside our ongoing assessment to identify children who require further support.
Children who do not meet the expected standard continue to receive targeted phonics teaching and are reassessed in Year 2.
Years 3 and 4
Phonics support continues beyond Year 2 for any child who has not yet secured the necessary decoding skills. Where appropriate, children may access Read Write Inc. Fresh Start or other targeted intervention.
Children who are secure in phonics increasingly focus on fluency, vocabulary and comprehension, enabling them to access increasingly challenging texts across the curriculum.
New Starters
Every child joining Grinling Gibbons is assessed promptly on entry, regardless of their year group or previous school. Their phonics and reading knowledge is used to identify their starting point, appropriate teaching group and any additional support required.
Assessment, Inclusion and Intervention
Assessment is an integral part of our phonics teaching. Staff regularly assess children’s knowledge and application of phonics to ensure that teaching responds to individual needs.
Children who require additional support receive targeted intervention, additional practice and appropriate adaptations. Our approach is “keep up, not catch up”, ensuring that gaps are addressed quickly and do not become barriers to reading.
Impact
The impact of our phonics curriculum is demonstrated through children’s ability to:
We evaluate the effectiveness of our phonics provision through ongoing assessment, RWI data, reading progress, intervention records, lesson observations, book scrutiny and the Phonics Screening Check.
Our aim is for every child to develop secure decoding skills, become a fluent reader and develop a lifelong love of reading.
The Phoenix federation uses the Literacy Tree, which is a book-based primary English planning resource. We believe that using engaging, language-rich and diverse texts, which are reflective of our community, inspire creativity and develop an enjoyment for writing.
As a federation we want our writing opportunities to be meaningful, and to be written with a clear audience and purpose in mind, whether the pieces we produce are short or long. Using books as a stimuli, we provide the opportunity to write for a range of purposes, for example to explain, persuade, inform or instruct. Wherever possible, writing is embedded within a text, piece of media or linked to a specific curriculum area.

PHONICS AND SPELLING
In the EYFS and Year 1, children receive a daily session in phonics. This teaches children to hear, say, read and write the full range of sounds needed to read and write independently.
From Year 2 onwards, children are taught the age-appropriate spelling patterns as outlined in the spelling appendix of the national curriculum.
All children are given a set of words to practise spelling, and from Year 1 onwards, these are tested once a week.
GRAMMAR AND PUNCTUATION
Wherever possible, grammar and punctuation is explored and taught within a real context: this may be done through a quality text that the children are reading, or it could be in the shared writing which all adults model as part of the teaching process.
HANDWRITING
In the Phoenix Federation children are taught to join their letters using the Letter-Join Programme. Children practise their handwriting regularly in order to develop confidence and fluency, and all adults model a joined handwriting script.
